result.topic_en: Draft on how the Fourier-coefficient integral $\int f(x)\cos n(x-a)\,dx$ behaves for the example $f=\varphi(x)\cos\psi(x)$; it shows that a function can be integrable while its trigonometric series diverges with unbounded terms, and that a series can converge densely for a function that is nowhere integrable.

methods.what: Asymptotic (stationary-phase type) estimate of the coefficient integral for $f=\varphi\cos\psi$; the leading term is of the order of $\varphi(\alpha)\psi'(\alpha)/\sqrt{2\psi''(\alpha)}$
Power-order assumptions on $\varphi$ and $\psi'$ near 0; the coefficient does not tend to zero if $\mu\ge 2\nu$
methods.quote:

so daß $\nu>0$ u $\mu \geqq 0$ sein muß

methods.what: Explanation: rapid sign changes of $f$ cancel the increments of $\int f$, while the factor $\cos n(x-a)$ makes them add up

items.english: Likewise one will find that if $x\psi'(x)$ (or, equivalently, $\psi x/\log x$) becomes infinitely large for infinitely small x, then $\varphi(x)$ can always be chosen so that $\varphi x$ is infinitely small, the amplitude becomes infinitely large, $\int f\,dx$ can be extended to x = 0, and the coefficient integral does not become infinitely small.

items.english: Despite f(x) being non-integrable throughout, between any two values, however close, there can lie infinitely many values at which the series converges.
